name: Small-cap and micro-cap equity
claim: Small caps compound at 20%+ a year if you hold long enough.
summary: Indian small-cap indices have produced multi-decade records that beat large caps — punctuated by drawdowns of 50–70% in 2008, 2013, 2018–19 and 2025. A 20% long-run figure is a best-case reading of the historical record, not a dependable planning assumption.

historical.statement: Certain multi-year windows did exceed 20% annualised; those windows ended in sharp reversals, and investors who bought near prior peaks waited years to recover. Survivorship of the index itself flatters the record — delisted and failed companies are absent.

contractual.statement: No contract exists. The entire return is price movement plus small dividends.

model.statement: No credible model supports a sustained 20% expected return for small caps. The defensible modelling position is a modest premium over large caps with far higher volatility — which is compensation for risk, not a free addition to return.

speculative.statement: Individual micro-cap stories of 10x exist and are heavily publicised; the base rate of stock-picking among micro-caps is not favourable and the segment has documented manipulation problems.

requiredConditions: A holding horizon you will actually tolerate through 50%+ drawdowns
Position sizes small enough that a total loss in one name is survivable
Awareness of low float, circuit limits and liquidity-driven price gaps
failureModes: Buying after a long run of outperformance and selling at the bottom
Concentration in one or two names
Treating index returns as achievable without surviving the path
taxNote: Long-term gains on listed equity: 12.5% above ₹1,25,000 a year with STT paid; short-term at the applicable rate — see the tax reference.
liquidityNote: Index-level liquidity is fine; individual micro-cap exits can take days and move the price.
effortNote: Low if index-based; high if stock-based.
bottomLine: Treat the historical 20%+ windows as evidence that the segment can run hot, not as a rate you can bank. Plan at a lower number and be pleasantly surprised.

name: P2P lending platforms
claim: Earn 12–15% lending to verified borrowers, monthly payouts, no market risk.
summary: Regulated peer-to-peer platforms intermediate loans at high borrower rates. Lender outcomes after defaults, platform fees, delayed recoveries and tax are far lower than the advertised gross rate — and 20%+ net to lenders is not established anywhere in the public record.

historical.statement: Platform-level realised lender returns are not published as audited series. Available evidence is platform-reported, which invites selection. Independent reconstructions of late-stage portfolios consistently show defaults eroding a large share of gross interest.

contractual.statement: Each loan carries a contractual rate that may exceed 20%. But the contract binds an unsecured borrower: the rate is compensation for expected default, and the recovery process is slow and partial.

model.statement: A stressed model — gross rate minus annual default and recovery costs, fees and tax — can land anywhere between large positive and negative depending on assumptions. The stress calculator on this site exists precisely because small default-rate changes dominate the outcome.

speculative.statement: Any promise of 20%+ net with 'safety' fails the basic credit arithmetic: safe borrowers do not pay such rates, and risky borrowers do not repay reliably on schedule.

requiredConditions: Thousands of small exposures to make default rates predictable
Tolerance for delayed and partial recoveries
A platform that survives — the intermediary itself is part of the risk
failureModes: One or two large exposures defaulting
Platform fee or model changes after you commit
Liquidity mismatch: your money is lent, not available
taxNote: Interest is taxed at your marginal slab rate; there is no concessional treatment for lending income.
liquidityNote: Low. Loans run to term; early exit depends on a thin secondary market.
bottomLine: A credit business wearing an investment costume. Model it with the stress calculator before a rupee is committed; assume a meaningful share of loans will underperform their schedule.

name: Category II AIFs — private credit funds
claim: Institutional-grade credit funds returning 16–20% with quarterly distributions.
summary: SEBI-regulated pooled vehicles that lend to mid-market and developer borrowers outside bank reach. Gross target yields are plausible; nets after fees, taxes, defaults and illiquidity are lower, and variance across funds is wide.

historical.statement: Fund-level realised series are private and reported to investors under confidentiality. Track records shown to prospects are selected. There is no public, audited, survivorship-free dataset of Indian private-credit fund returns.

contractual.statement: The underlying loans carry contractual coupons well above bank lending rates. Whether lenders receive them depends on borrower performance, security enforcement and fund-level sequencing.

model.statement: Net outcomes are highly sensitive to default timing: one large impaired position in an eight-asset fund can consume several years of spread.

speculative.statement: No evidence supports 20% net-of-fee returns as anything other than exceptional case-by-case outcomes.

requiredConditions: Minimums are typically ₹1 crore for AIF units
Ability to assess the manager's credit process, not just presented returns
Acceptance of multi-year lock-ins with no secondary market
failureModes: Concentration in one borrower group (recurrent in Indian credit funds)
Valuation smoothing hiding stress until exit
Fee load (management plus carry) on moderate gross spreads
taxNote: Taxation depends on fund structure and unit status; long-term rates apply to eligible units after the statutory holding period.
effortNote: High — this is manager selection, not product selection.
bottomLine: A legitimate asset class for investors who can underwrite credit processes and tolerate multi-year locks. The advertised yield is the starting point of the analysis, not the answer.

name: SME IPOs and high-subscription issues
claim: Listing gains of 50–200% are routine in the SME segment.
summary: Some SME issues list at multiples of their issue price; many of those gains are not realisable for ordinary allottees, and the segment has documented manipulation and post-listing collapse. SEBI has repeatedly tightened SME IPO norms for this reason.

historical.statement: Listing pops are real and documented. Retention of the pop is not: thin floats, circuit limits and demand that evaporates after listing mean paper gains frequently cannot be exited at quoted prices.

contractual.statement: No contractual return; the issue price is a sale, not a promise.

model.statement: No model supports routine 50%+ outcomes. Reported averages are dominated by small floats and survivorship in news coverage.

speculative.statement: Treating an auction-shaped segment as a systematic 20%+ strategy ignores that the winning bidders are often the sellers' counter-parties at inflated prices.

requiredConditions: Direct-seller discipline: sell into strength, not after circuit breaks
Awareness that allotment is probabilistic
Understanding of the SME platform's separate rules and penalties
failureModes: Holding post-listing when the float normalises
Consortium manipulation collapsing the price floor
Allotment lottery skewing results
taxNote: Listing gains are short-term capital gains taxed at the applicable rate; the 12.5% long-term rate applies only after the holding period with STT paid.
liquidityNote: Very poor after listing despite the 'listed' label.
bottomLine: A market microstructure story, not an investment process. If you participate, decide your exit before you bid.

name: Equity derivatives trading (options and futures)
claim: 20–50% monthly returns from options strategies with proper discipline.
summary: The most aggressively marketed high-return claim in India. SEBI's own studies of individual equity-derivatives traders found that the large majority incurred net losses over multi-year windows, with aggregate losses running into lakhs of crores.

historical.statement: SEBI's published research on individual traders in the equity-derivatives segment found that over 90% incurred net losses across a three-year period, with aggregate net losses of roughly ₹1.8 lakh crore. The segment's realised history for retail participants is a history of loss.

contractual.statement: A derivative is a zero-sum contract: every rupee of a winner's gross profit is a rupee of another participant's gross loss, before costs. No yield is produced by the contract itself.

model.statement: Option-selling strategies show high win rates with fat left tails; buyers show the reverse. Neither has a model-implied 20% monthly edge — the arithmetic of compounding 20% monthly would make any such trader the owner of the entire market within years.

speculative.statement: Screenshot-driven 'returns' omit position sizing, financing, failed strategies and survivorship. Acting on them is the mechanism by which their producers monetise an audience.

requiredConditions: If pursued institutionally: legal, pricing and risk infrastructure far beyond a retail terminal
Recognition that the published base rate is a loss, not a draw
failureModes: Loss-chasing after drawdowns
Short-premium strategies meeting a gap move
Cost, tax and margin drag compounding the base-rate disadvantage
taxNote: Speculative business income (intraday) and non-speculative treatment for delivery and, in specified cases, derivatives — taxed at slab rates; classification and turnover rules matter.
liquidityNote: High for index products — which cuts both ways.
effortNote: High, and negatively compensated on average.
bottomLine: The clearest documented case on this site of a marketed high-return claim contradicted by the regulator's own data. Read SEBI's study before considering any strategy that claims otherwise.

name: Unlisted and pre-IPO equity
claim: Buy the next big listing at a discount to its IPO price.
summary: Unlisted shares trade in bilateral, lightly regulated markets with appraisal-based pricing, long settlement and real legal restrictions. The discount to a hoped-for listing price is compensation for illiquidity and for the chance that no listing happens on the hoped-for terms — or at all.

historical.statement: Case histories of large gains and large wipeouts exist; no survivorship-free public dataset of unlisted returns exists. Platform price-tape data is self-reported.

contractual.statement: No contractual return; some structures involve option-like arrangements whose enforceability is itself a risk.

model.statement: Valuations rest on negotiated or platform-quoted levels, not continuous markets, so 'return' is a paper figure until a genuine sale occurs.

speculative.statement: Professional pre-IPO investors can earn very high IRRs — with information access, diligence and diversification unavailable to most individuals.

requiredConditions: Legal diligence on transferability (companies restrict share transfers; some instruments require approvals)
Horizon measured in years with no ability to exit on demand
Acceptance that price quotes can be unfillable
failureModes: Buying from an informal dealer with no settlement protection
Listing postponed indefinitely
Valuation collapses from the last quoted round
taxNote: Unlisted share gains: the applicable long-term rate after the 24-month holding period; short-term at slab rates. Check the dated rules before transacting.
liquidityNote: Very low; settlement is manual and counterparty-dependent.
bottomLine: For most investors this is a headline, not an asset class. Where pursued, size it as capital that may be locked for years.

name: Real-estate redevelopment and development
summary: Genuine high-IRR projects exist in real estate — for developers with local expertise, capital and legal execution capability. The IRRs come from the development business, not from owning property, and failed projects show symmetric downside.

historical.statement: Completed, well-bought, well-sold projects frequently clear 20%+ IRRs. The same projects, delayed two years or bought at peak input costs (2022 steel, 2024 land), often return little or less than zero.

contractual.statement: No contractual return; revenues depend on future sales prices and approvals.

model.statement: Project IRRs are legitimately computable from cash-flow models. The assumptions — approval timelines, sales velocity, input costs, financing cost — are where the return lives or dies, and each is outside an investor's control.

speculative.statement: Pooled 'fractional development' platforms extrapolate developer returns to passive investors while abstracting execution risk, delays and counterparty failure.

requiredConditions: Local knowledge of approvals, title and micro-market pricing
Capital reserves for overruns and delay
Clear legal structure for any profit-share investment
failureModes: Approval delay doubling financing cost
Title defects emerging mid-project
Sales prices deflating while costs are fixed
taxNote: Project profits typically taxed as business income for developers; passive property returns have their own capital-gains and rent regimes.
liquidityNote: None until completion and sale — years.
bottomLine: Real estate's high returns are paid to the developer's skill and capital, not to the asset. Investors seeking that return passively are financing someone else's business at their risk, not buying the return.

name: Agro and natural-asset investment schemes
claim: 20–30% from teak, sandalwood, emu farming and farmland schemes.
summary: A recurring category in Indian enforcement history: schemes promising high returns from crops, trees or livestock in which the investor never holds the asset or receives its output. The recurring mechanic is upfront money against a distant payoff that depends entirely on the promoter.

historical.statement: The realised history of this category is dominated by failed or fraudulent schemes documented by regulators and courts — from plantation bonds of the 1990s to more recent pooled-tree and livestock schemes.

contractual.statement: Where the 'return' is contractual, the contract usually violates securities or collective-investment law, which removes the very protections it appears to offer.

model.statement: Promoter projections of tree or livestock yields are unaudited, ignore survival and disease rates, and assume fixed sale prices decades out.

speculative.statement: Legitimate agribusiness returns exist for operating farmers and processors — the participation structure, not the sector, is what determines whether an investor sees them.

requiredConditions: Direct ownership or verifiable legal title to land, trees or produce
Unrelated third-party verification of yields and prices
If it is a pooled scheme: registration with SEBI or another regulator, checkable today
failureModes: Promoter insolvency before the payoff period
No enforceable claim on any physical asset
Scheme classified as unregistered collective investment
taxNote: Agricultural income has special constitutional and tax treatment; returns from non-agricultural pooled schemes are ordinary income in the promoter's hands and taxable recoveries at best for investors.
bottomLine: This is the single category on this site where the prior probability of the scheme being legitimate is lowest. Verify registration and title before anything else, and expect that most high-return schemes in this space are neither.

name: Crypto assets and tokens
summary: No cash flows, no issuer, no legal claim — the entire return is price change. Historical price records show both enormous multi-year gains and 70–80% drawdowns. Indian tax law is deliberately harsh: 30% flat on gains, 1% TDS on transfers, and losses that cannot offset other income.

historical.statement: Multi-year windows exist where holding major crypto assets beat every conventional asset class; adjacent windows lost most of their value. Any 'expected' figure derived from the record is dominated by survivorship among thousands of failed tokens.

contractual.statement: There is no contract, no counterparty and no yield — anything marketed as 'earn' is itself a credit exposure to an unregulated intermediary.

model.statement: There is no accepted, validated valuation model that produces a 20% expected-return figure for any digital asset. Long-run estimates are the product of assumptions about adoption that cannot be evidenced today.

speculative.statement: The honest statement is that the future price is unknowable and the asset is a speculation whose expected value has no defensible estimate.

requiredConditions: Self-custody competence if custody risk matters to you
Recognition of Indian tax treatment before entry (no loss set-off)
Position sizing consistent with a possible 80% drawdown
failureModes: Exchange or custody failure
Token collapse to zero
Selling in a drawdown to meet tax on gains held in assets
taxNote: Transfers are taxed at 30% flat on gains under the virtual-digital-asset regime, 1% TDS applies on transfers, and losses cannot be set off against other income.
liquidityNote: 24/7 markets for majors; effectively zero for most tokens.
effortNote: Moderate to high; custody and tax compliance are non-trivial.
bottomLine: An explicit speculation. The arithmetic of Indian tax treatment means gross gains erase fast, and nothing in the historical record supports a dependable 20% figure.

name: Leveraged index futures and structured leverage
claim: Amplify index returns 3–5x with futures or leveraged products.
summary: Leverage multiplies outcomes symmetrically before costs and asymmetrically after them. The index's drift is unchanged; the cost of financing, rollover and the forced-exit risk of margin calls make leveraged outcomes worse than n × unleveraged for most holders.

historical.statement: Over multi-year windows, levered and inverse products in global markets have systematically underperformed their stated multiple because of volatility drag and daily rebalancing — a documented structural result, not a market opinion.

contractual.statement: Futures price the cost of carry; there is no yield to collect, only basis to track.

model.statement: The claim '3x the return' fails mathematically: compounding of a volatile path at 3x leverage produces materially less than 3× the terminal multiple, and paths ending below the borrow cost produce magnified losses.

speculative.statement: Tactical leverage can help a trader with demonstrated timing; the base rate from SEBI's derivatives data shows what usually happens.

requiredConditions: Explicit leverage policy with hard caps
Liquidity to meet margin calls without forced sales of core assets
Cost tracking: rollover, brokerage, financing
failureModes: Margin call at the worst point of the path
Volatility drag silently compounding against you
Position sized as if the leverage claim were linear
taxNote: Derivative income is generally non-speculative business income for tax (exceptaggressive intraday classification); taxes fall due on profits regardless of reinvestment.
bottomLine: Leverage is a financing decision, not a return source. The index's expected return does not change when you borrow against it — only the variance and the odds of being forced out do.

name: PMS, AIFs and star fund managers
claim: This manager has beaten the market at 20%+ for years — join the fund.
summary: Some managers do beat indices over long periods. The questions are whether the record survives fees and survivorship, whether you can access the surviving managers, and whether outperformance persists once money follows. Public evidence on persistence is weak.

historical.statement: Individual managers have long records of genuine outperformance. At the category level, survivorship tips the reported average: funds that underperformed are closed and deleted from the record you are shown.

contractual.statement: No contractual return is ever promised by a genuine manager — and any that is promised is a red flag.

model.statement: Academic evidence on performance persistence is weak: past winners do not reliably remain winners after fees. Expectation should start at the market return minus costs, adjusted for exposure.

speculative.statement: Investing in a genuinely skilled manager early can deliver exceptional returns — the difficulty is distinguishing skill from luck and access from salesmanship.

requiredConditions: Records verified against audited NAV series, not presented decks
Full fee structure understood (management plus performance fee)
Alignment: manager's own money in the strategy
failureModes: Capacity: a small fund's edge does not survive a large fund
Style drift after fundraising
Survivorship in the peer set you compare against
taxNote: Tax treatment of PMS (direct holding, per-transaction) differs from funds (per-unit); confirm the dated rules.
liquidityNote: PMS: high (listed holdings). AIFs: low, lock-ins.
effortNote: High — due diligence is the work.
bottomLine: Skill exists and is hard to identify. Buy evidence and process, not a narrative — and model returns net of every fee, because that is the only return you keep.

name: Invoice discounting and trade-finance platforms
claim: 12–18% from short-duration, self-liquidating invoice financing — safer than equity.
summary: Financing receivables of real businesses at a discount is a genuine credit activity. Platform-intermediated retail versions carry invoice-authenticity, settlement and platform risks that the short tenor obscures. 'Self-liquidating' describes a hope, not a mechanism.

historical.statement: The TReDS exchange system for MSME receivables provides a regulated, invoice-verified benchmark. Platform-intermediated retail variants operate in a newer, less-verified space with no long public loss record — which cuts both ways.

contractual.statement: The discount rate is set in the financing documents; whether the receivable exists and is paid is the credit question.

model.statement: Short tenors (30–120 days) support high annualised yields from small discounts, but a single default period can erase a year's spread on that capital.

speculative.statement: No evidence supports a 20%+ net return endurance claim outside of operations with genuine underwriting.

requiredConditions: Verification that invoices are real and unpaid (e.g. on a regulated exchange)
Diversification across many obligors and industries
Legal ability to enforce against the paying company, not just the platform
failureModes: Fabricated invoices (a documented fraud pattern in trade finance globally)
Platform or intermediary failure with your money mid-cycle
Disputed receivables stalling recovery for months
taxNote: Discount income is interest-like, taxed at slab rates.
liquidityNote: Funds recycle on each invoice's tenor, but principal is at risk during it.
bottomLine: Real finance, real risks. Prefer structures with exchange-verified invoices and obligor credit, and treat platform marketing as the least reliable input in the decision.

name: Owning a business
claim: Nothing beats a business for wealth creation.
summary: Historically accurate and structurally different from every other item on this page: returns to business ownership come from operated capital — pricing power, reinvestment, operating leverage — and depend on the owner's execution, not on a market's re-rating.

historical.statement: The survivors of every economy's business population create the large fortunes. The base includes business owners who lost their invested capital; entrepreneurship's return distribution is extremely wide.

contractual.statement: No promise exists; the owner is the residual claimant.

model.statement: Return on capital employed is a real, measurable quantity: a business earning 25% after-tax on capital and reinvesting at that rate compounds at 25% until competition or scale intervenes.

speculative.statement: Projections in business plans are marketing; bankable plans assume competition arrives late.

requiredConditions: Capital that can be lost without ruin
Operational capability or honest partners who have it
Reinvestment discipline: returns compound only if profits are redeployed at high rates
failureModes: Good business, wrong price
Key-person dependency
Reinvesting into a business whose unit economics have quietly declined
taxNote: Business income at slab rates; structured exits through capital gains have separate rules. Compliance load is ongoing.
liquidityNote: Usually none, until a sale that may take years to arrange.
bottomLine: The most reliable engine of large wealth in the historical record — priced in years of work, family risk and no liquidity. It is not a 'passive high-return avenue', and comparisons to passive investing are category errors.
